name: Trigeminal neuralgia
presentation: An older patient describes electric shocks in the cheek and jaw that last a second or two, come in volleys, and are set off by chewing, brushing the teeth, a breath of cold air or a light touch to a particular spot on the face. Between attacks there is no pain and the examination is normal. In a young woman with bilateral or persistent pain, sensory loss or other cranial nerve signs, multiple sclerosis or a tumor must be sought.

deficits.distribution: V2 and/or V3 divisions, rarely V1
deficits.sign: Paroxysmal lancinating pain with trigger zones; no pain between attacks
Normal sensation and corneal reflex in classic cases; any deficit suggests a structural cause
Facial spasm with the pain (tic douloureux)

reasoning: In most patients the trigeminal root is compressed and indented at its entry into the pons by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery, occasionally a vein, which demyelinates the large touch fibers at the root entry zone where central myelin gives way to peripheral myelin. The demyelinated fibers become hyperexcitable and generate ectopic bursts, and cross-talk between light-touch fibers and neighboring pain fibers means that a trivial touch stimulus is felt as an explosion of pain, which explains the trigger zones and the sparing of sensation between attacks. The nerve is the uncrossed sensory supply of the ipsilateral face, so the pain is strictly unilateral and confined to one or two divisions, most often the maxillary and mandibular. Because the second-order neurons for facial pain lie in the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the medulla, a demyelinating plaque along the root fibers as they enter the pons or descend in the spinal tract can produce the same pain, which is why multiple sclerosis is the commonest cause in the young and is the explanation for bilateral cases. A cerebellopontine angle tumor compresses the root from outside and adds sensory loss, a depressed corneal reflex or other cranial nerve signs.

imagingFindings.finding: Superior cerebellar artery loop contacting and distorting the trigeminal root at the pontine entry zone on thin-section heavily T2-weighted images (CISS/FIESTA) with MRA.
FLAIR-bright plaque in the pontine trigeminal root entry zone or along the spinal tract.
Meningioma, epidermoid or schwannoma compressing the nerve; epidermoids restrict diffusion.

commonCauses: Neurovascular compression by the superior cerebellar artery
Herpes zoster (postherpetic, continuous rather than paroxysmal)

mimics.name: Dental pain
mimics.howToDistinguish: Continuous, localized to a tooth, tender to percussion

mimics.name: Cluster headache
mimics.howToDistinguish: Orbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with autonomic features

mimics.name: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain in the throat and ear triggered by swallowing

mimics.name: Postherpetic neuralgia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Constant burning with allodynia after a rash, usually V1

management: Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is first-line and its response supports the diagnosis
MRI with thin brainstem sequences in every patient to exclude MS and tumor and to show vascular contact
Microvascular decompression or ablative procedures (radiofrequency, gamma knife) for drug-resistant cases

imagingHint.label: trigeminal root entry zone at the lateral pons
